title: Reactions of Alkenes
page_title: Reactions of Alkenes - CIE A Level Chemistry Revision Notes

blocks.md:
- Alkenes are very useful compounds as they can undergo many types of reactions
- They can therefore be used as starting molecules when making new compounds

- **Electrophilic** **addition** is the addition of an electrophile to a double bond
- The C-C double bond is broken, and a new single bond is formed from each of the two carbon atoms
- Electrophilic addition reactions include the addition of:

  - Hydrogen (also known as **hydrogenation** **reaction**)
  - Steam (H<sub>2</sub>O (g))
  - Hydrogen halide (HX)
  - Halogen

blocks.alt: Diagram illustrating electrophilic addition reactions: hydrogenation, steam addition, hydrogen halides, and halogens with alkenes forming various products.

blocks.md:
- Alkenes can also be **oxidised **by **acidified potassium manganate(VII) **(KMnO<sub>4</sub>) which is a very powerful **oxidising agent**
- Alkenes can be oxidised by both **hot** and **cold **KMnO<sub>4</sub> which will result in different products being formed

  - When shaken with **cold dilute KMnO**<sub>**4**</sub> the **pale purple **solution turns **colourless **and the product is a **diol**
  - When alkenes are reacted with **hot concentrated KMnO**<sub>**4**</sub> the conditions are harsher causing the C-C double bond to completely break
  - The O-H groups in the diol formed are further oxidised to **ketones**, **aldehydes**, **carboxylic acids **or **carbon dioxide gas**
  - The actual products formed depend on what is bonded to the carbon atoms in the alkene

blocks.alt: Diagram showing oxidation reactions of alkenes with KMnO₄, forming diol, carbon dioxide, aldehyde, carboxylic acid, and ketone.
blocks.caption: Alkenes can be oxidised by cold dilute and hot concentrated KMnO₄ to give different products

blocks.md: - The reactions of alkenes with hot concentrated KMnO<sub>4</sub> can be used to determine the position of the double bond in larger alkenes

blocks.text: Predicting the position of double bonds formed

blocks.alt: Diagram showing oxidation of carbon atoms based on their bonding: to CO2 with two H-atoms, COOH with one H-atom/alkyl group, and C=O with two alkyl groups.
blocks.caption: The above reactions can be used to predict where the double bond in a larger molecule is

blocks.label: Worked Example
blocks.md:
What are the products of the oxidation of 2-methylprop-1-ene with hot, concentrated acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub> (aq)?

**Answer:**

The products are propanone (a ketone), carbon dioxide and water

![Chemical reaction diagram showing an alkene reacting with oxygen and hot concentrated KMnO4 to produce a ketone, CO2, and H2O.](assets/de8eb64a758e-3-2-hydrocarbons-oxidation-of-2-methylprop-1-ene.png)

blocks.label: Worked Example
blocks.md:
The oxidation of an alkane produces carbon dioxide gas, water and propanoic acid. Identify the alkene.

**Answer:**

The alkene is 1-butene

![Chemical reaction diagram showing oxidation of an alkene forming CO2 and propanoic acid, identifying the alkene as 1-butene with structural formulas.](assets/541bec6280cc-3-2-hydrocarbons-oxidation-of-1-butene.png)

- **Addition polymerisation** is the reaction of many monomers containing at least one double C-C bond to form the long-chain polymers as the only product

  - **Monomers** are small, reactive molecules that react together to make the polymer
  - A **polymer** is a long-chain molecule made up of many **repeating units **(monomers)
- In an addition polymerisation reaction, the C-C double bond is broken to link together the monomers and form a polymer
- This is a common method of making **plastics**

blocks.alt: Diagram showing ethene polymerisation to poly(ethene) with repeating units. Includes chemical structures and a section of polymer made of four monomers.
blocks.caption: The polymer backbone consists of a carbon chain with monomers that contain 2 carbon atoms

blocks.alt: Diagram showing the polymerisation of propene to poly(propene) with repeating units, illustrating a polymer section of four monomers.
blocks.caption: The polymer backbone consists of a carbon chain with monomers that contain 2 carbon atoms with the methyl group, from the propane monomer, as a side chain

blocks.md:
- Other alkenes and **substituted **alkenes can also polymerise to make polymers with different **properties**

  - E.g. poly(chloroethene), also known as PVC is the most versatile plastic used

blocks.alt: Chemical reaction of chloroethene (vinyl chloride) forming poly(chloroethene) or PVC, showing structural formulas and labelled chemical names.
blocks.caption: Poly(chloroethene) is used as plastic
